candidates.headline: One-token-per-iteration decode demand does not imply the same bound holds for multi-token steps
candidates.claim: The at-most-one-page-group-per-tensor bound, and the background-thread overlap built on it, assume decode produces exactly one token per iteration. Steps that add several tokens could cross page boundaries and need more mappings than the overlap prepared. The paper does not discuss this case.
candidates.paper_fact: For a request in the decode phase, the number of new page-groups required is at most one per virtual tensor. This is because each iteration produces only one output token for a request.
candidates.premise: General knowledge: speculative decoding verifies several draft tokens per iteration, and chunked prefill processes a block of prompt tokens per iteration. Either can add more tokens than fit in the already mapped page-group.
candidates.inference: The step API itself takes arbitrary sequence lengths and computes prefill demand as (s+t-1)/t, so it can map more pages. But the decode latency-hiding in §6.1.1 relies on knowing demand one iteration ahead from a single-token increment. A larger step could make the next iteration's mappings fall back to the synchronous path, which costs about 5 ms per request for Yi-34B.
candidates.toy_example: Illustrative only, not a measurement: if a page-group holds 256 tokens and an iteration adds 8 tokens at position 252, the step crosses a page boundary. The same crossing can occur in several requests at once.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If a framework uses multi-token steps, the decode overlap may not hide mapping latency, and iteration latency spikes like those in the without-overlap curve of Figure 12 could reappear.
candidates.critical_link: Latency hiding depends on predicting next-iteration demand from a one-token increment, which multi-token steps invalidate.
necessary_conditions: The serving framework runs multi-token steps in decode-like iterations
The added tokens cross a page-group boundary
defeaters: The background thread prefetches enough page-groups ahead
Large page-groups make boundary crossings rare
The framework calls step with accurate lengths before each iteration so mapping is correct, only slower
do_not_infer: Do not infer that step would map memory incorrectly for multi-token steps
Do not infer that the paper claims support for speculative decoding
Do not infer that the paper measured any slowdown for these cases

candidates.headline: Cached idle page-groups conflict with the claim that deferred reclamation keeps unmap cost off the critical path near capacity
candidates.claim: Deferred reclamation defers the unmap and release work rather than removing it. The paper triggers reclamation only below a threshold and delegates it to a background thread. Near serving capacity, idle pages held in finished slots reduce free memory for admission, so reclamation is more likely to run during load. The paper gives no evidence on whether that work stays hidden.
candidates.paper_fact: we trigger memory reclamation only when the number of page-groups cached in vAttention falls below a certain threshold (e.g., less than 10% of GPU memory).
candidates.premise: Memory held in cached slots is unavailable for other allocations until reclaimed. Unmap plus release at 2MB costs about 34µs + 23µs per call (Table 3). A step that needs memory must wait if the background thread has not freed it yet.
candidates.inference: Under memory pressure the reclamation cost returns, and it is multiplied across 2N tensors. If the background thread lags, the cost can surface as a latency spike in the step that needs the memory. The paper evaluates a single 16K prefill and does not test this regime.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: for Yi-34B (N=60, so 120 tensors), reclaiming one 2MB page-group row across all tensors would be about 120 x (34+23) µs ≈ 6.8 ms of unmap and release calls. If this ran synchronously in one step, it would be comparable to the 5 ms latency the paper reports for mapping a single request's new page-groups.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If the system runs near memory capacity so that cached pages approach the threshold, reclamation runs repeatedly. Whether it overlaps with compute then depends on the background thread keeping up.
candidates.critical_link: The unmap and release cost is deferred, not removed. Its placement on or off the critical path under pressure is not evaluated.

The background thread is slower than the demand for freed memory
A step must wait for reclaimed memory before it can proceed
defeaters: The background thread reclaims fast enough to overlap with the 10s-100s of ms iteration time
The load never nears the threshold because the example threshold is generous
Smaller page-groups (64KB) make each call cheaper: 2-4µs for vMemRelease in Table 3

Do not infer that the 10% threshold is tuned; the paper says 'e.g.'
Do not infer a specific interaction with the paper's failure and preemption path; the paper does not describe one
The quoted threshold wording ('number of page-groups cached ... falls below') is ambiguous as written; the paper may mean free memory, so the exact trigger is unclear

candidates.headline: Virtual contiguity of the KV cache does not guarantee low physical fragmentation
candidates.claim: Keeping the KV cache virtually contiguous with on-demand physical mapping only reduces fragmentation if the physical page-group is small. With stock CUDA VMM (2MB pages), each of the 2N per-layer K/V tensors still wastes a partially filled large page per request. The paper's own batch-size result shows this cost.
candidates.paper_fact: Use of large pages can waste physical memory due to internal fragmentation.
candidates.premise: A virtual tensor backed by fixed-size physical pages wastes, on average, part of the last page of every request's sub-tensor. Waste per request therefore scales with page size times the number of independently backed tensors (2N), not with the number of requests alone.
candidates.inference: The 'no fragmentation' property comes from decoupling plus small page-groups, not from decoupling alone. Without the modified driver (64KB to 256KB), stock CUDA 2MB pages leave much of the fragmentation problem in place, and the paper itself reports lower max batch size with 2MB pages than with 64KB pages.
candidates.toy_example: Illustrative arithmetic, not a measurement: with 2N = 120 tensors and 2MB page-groups, each request can strand up to about one page per tensor in the last partially filled page. With 64KB page-groups the bound is 32x smaller.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If a deployment must use stock CUDA 2MB pages and runs a throughput-oriented, high-batch workload, physical fragmentation would cap batch size below what PagedAttention-style small blocks allow. This holds unless tensor slicing is used.
candidates.critical_link: Fragmentation waste is set by physical page-group granularity times tensor count, not by virtual contiguity.
necessary_conditions: Physical backing granularity is 2MB (stock cuMemCreate)
The workload is memory-capacity-limited so that wasted pages reduce batch size
Per-layer K and V remain separate virtual tensors
defeaters: The modified driver with 64KB to 256KB page-groups is available
Tensor slicing across layers is used (the paper states it reduces fragmentation to 1/N)
The workload is latency-bound with small batches, where the paper says 2MB pages are good enough
do_not_infer: Do not infer that vAttention fragments more than PagedAttention in general; the paper reports 64KB pages approach vLLM's block sizes.
Do not infer that 2MB pages hurt online latency-constrained serving; the paper says they are good enough there.
Do not infer a quantified fragmentation figure from this critique; none is measured here.

candidates.headline: Abundant virtual address space does not guarantee the pre-reservation always fits
candidates.claim: The design reserves virtual space of 2N x B x S per worker up front, with S computed at the model's maximum context length. The paper's 'always plentiful' conclusion rests on one configuration. It mixes per-process and total address-space figures, so the margin shrinks as B, N, H or L grow.
candidates.paper_fact: Therefore, the total virtual memory requirement for 60 layers is 120 buffers of 100GB each (12TB total).
candidates.premise: A process has a fixed user virtual address range (128TB on a 48-bit system). Reservation size scales linearly with batch size B, layer count N, KV heads H, head dimension D and context length L. Worker processes do not pool each other's address space.
candidates.inference: The paper compares the per-worker 12TB requirement with a 256TB 'total' across two TP workers. The binding limit for a reservation inside one process is that process's own user range, not the sum over workers. The statement that available space 'grows with the number of workers' therefore does not widen the per-worker margin.
candidates.toy_example: Illustrative arithmetic using the paper's formula, not a measurement: Yi-34B TP-2 at B=500 needs 12TB. Scaling B to 5500 with everything else fixed gives 12TB x 11 = 132TB, above a 128TB per-process user range.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If a deployment raises B, uses a model with more KV heads per worker or a longer context, or uses fewer workers per model, the up-front reservation could fail or leave little headroom. The paper's 12TB vs 128TB margin does not cover such configurations.
candidates.critical_link: The reservation uses worst-case L for all B request slots and is checked against a per-process limit, so it scales with B x L x 2N.

Reservation is sized at maximum context length for all B slots

candidates.headline: Fixed per-request slots at offset reqId*S do not imply or guarantee compatibility with any unmodified attention kernel
candidates.claim: Pre-reserving fixed slots of size S per request makes every request's cache live at a stable offset, but it leaves holes when a request in the middle of the batch exits. Kernels must then accept a batch-index indirection between Q and the KV cache (such as FlashAttention's cache_batch_idx). The 'works with unmodified kernels' framing is therefore conditional on that API existing.
candidates.paper_fact: This layout is not supported by implementations that expect the query (Q) and KV cache to be of the same size in batch
candidates.premise: A request's slot index is fixed by reqId, while its position in the current Q batch changes as continuous batching adds and removes requests. A kernel can read the right slot only if it accepts an explicit batch-index mapping or strided addressing.
candidates.inference: Contiguity avoids Block-Tables, but the slot layout shifts a compatibility requirement from a paging-aware kernel to a batch-index-aware kernel. Kernels without such an argument would need a copy, a repack, or a code change. This is supported by the paper's own note that FlashInfer lacked stride support.
candidates.toy_example: Illustrative, not a measurement: with B=4 slots, if requests in slots 0 and 2 finish and only slots 1 and 3 remain active, Q has batch size 2 while the KV tensor has batch size 4. A kernel that indexes KV by Q's batch position reads the wrong slots.
candidates.conditional_consequence: A new kernel that assumes dense, equal-sized Q and KV batch dimensions and offers no cache_batch_idx-like argument cannot be dropped in without extra work, despite avoiding Block-Tables.
candidates.critical_link: Whether the target kernel exposes a batch-index (or equivalent stride) mapping from Q to KV cache slots.

The kernel assumes equal Q and KV batch dimensions

candidates.headline: A split between PyTorch's pool and vAttention's pre-allocated pages does not guarantee that free KV pages can serve activation demand
candidates.claim: vAttention pre-allocates physical pages at init, while activations come from the standard PyTorch caching allocator. The paper does not say how GPU memory is divided between them. candidates.inference: The activation allocator can fail while the KV page pool still has unmapped or cached pages. Activation memory grows with the tokens processed per iteration (for example, large prefill chunks). The paper reports prefill up to 192K, so these configurations evidently fit.

candidates.inference: Between exit and reclamation, an idle reqId holds physical page-groups sized to the previous request's context length, and a later short request that inherits the slot also inherits those pages. This residual retention is inferred from the deferred-reclamation description; the paper does not measure it.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: R1 reaches 100 page-groups per tensor and exits. A short R2 needing 5 page-groups reuses the slot. Up to 95 page-groups stay mapped but unused until reclamation triggers.

candidates.headline: A failure return from step does not imply or guarantee forward progress
candidates.claim: The step API only reports failure when physical pages cannot be mapped. Whether the system then makes progress depends on a preemption policy that the serving framework must supply. The paper describes only a recompute-style default and does not evaluate its cost.
candidates.paper_fact: If vAttention cannot satisfy the memory demand, it returns with a failure in response to which a serving framework can preempt one or more requests to allow forward progress
candidates.premise: General knowledge: a status code of -1 only reports that mapping failed. Progress requires some component to free pages by evicting or recomputing requests, and that choice affects latency, wasted work and fairness. Recompute-style preemption discards KV state that must be rebuilt through prefill.
candidates.inference: The paper says a framework 'can' preempt, so progress is conditional on that policy existing and choosing victims whose freed pages cover the shortfall. The artifact guarantees contiguity and on-demand mapping. It does not guarantee liveness or bounded cost under memory pressure.
candidates.toy_example: Illustrative only, not a measurement: suppose step fails and the framework preempts the shortest request, which frees fewer pages than the failing request needs. The next step call fails again, and the loop can repeat or thrash.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If the framework's preemption policy is naive or absent, then under memory pressure the system can stall or repeatedly recompute work, even though the memory mapping itself is correct.
candidates.critical_link: Failure is signalled by vAttention, but victim selection and the cost of recompute live outside it and are not evaluated.

The serving framework's preemption policy is naive, absent, or frees too few pages

A policy that frees enough pages in one preemption
Workloads that never reach memory capacity
do_not_infer: Do not infer that the paper reports stalls or livelock
Do not infer that vLLM's default preemption is ineffective
Do not infer that step failure is frequent in the paper's experiments

candidates.headline: Iterations lasting 10s-100s of ms does not guarantee that background page mapping stays hidden on faster hardware or with more parallelism
candidates.claim: The overlap works only while the next iteration's mapping work finishes inside the current iteration. The paper justifies this with a typical iteration latency of 10s-100s of ms. That is a property of the evaluated A100 setups, not of the mechanism.
candidates.paper_fact: Since per-iteration latency is typically in the range of 10s-100s of milliseconds, the background thread has enough time to prepare physical memory mappings for an iteration before it starts executing.
candidates.premise: Faster GPUs, smaller models, and higher tensor-parallel degree shorten decode iterations. Per-call driver latency is a CPU and driver cost that does not shrink with GPU speed.
candidates.inference: If iteration time falls while per-iteration map work stays the same or rises, the margin shrinks. The paper reports H100 throughput in Figure 11 but runs the hiding ablation (Figure 12) only on A100.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement. Suppose an iteration takes 8ms while 3 requests each need 2N = 60 calls at about 40us. That is about 7.2ms of mapping, which barely fits. Four crossing requests would be about 9.6ms and would not fit.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If iteration time drops below aggregate map time, the overlap no longer hides the cost, and step() latency reappears as spikes in decode iterations.
candidates.critical_link: The claim that the thread 'has enough time' rests on an iteration-time regime that was assumed, not tested on other hardware or at higher TP.

candidates.headline: Deferred reclamation with reqId reuse does not guarantee that prefill needs no physical mapping
candidates.claim: Reusing a finished request's reqId removes prefill-time mapping only when a finished slot is available and already holds enough page-groups. A burst of arrivals, or a new prompt longer than the old slot's context, still requires mapping on the prefill path. Eager allocation is prepared for only one reqId at a time.
candidates.paper_fact: Therefore, new allocations are required only if R2’s context length is higher than R1.
candidates.premise: A reused slot's mapped size equals what its previous occupant reached. A new prompt larger than that needs the difference mapped. A slot can be reused only after some earlier request has exited.
candidates.inference: The benefit is bounded by how often a slot is available and by the gap between old and new context lengths. Under a burst of simultaneous arrivals, or when prompts are longer than the freed slots, the remaining mapping falls back on the one eagerly prepared reqId or on synchronous mapping.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: suppose 4 requests arrive before any has exited. Then 0 slots hold reusable pages, and only 1 reqId has been eagerly prepared. The other 3 would need mapping at prefill unless the background thread has caught up.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If arrivals cluster (offline start, bursty traffic) or length variance is high, a larger share of prefills still pay mapping cost. The reported deferred-reclamation gain then shrinks toward the cost of whatever the single eager reqId cannot cover.
candidates.critical_link: Reuse hit rate is determined by exit-before-arrival ordering and by the old-versus-new length relation. The paper's wording does not quantify either.
necessary_conditions: Arrival rate is not far above exit rate over short windows
Freed slots hold at least as many page-groups as the next prompt needs
The background thread finishes eager mapping before the next arrival
defeaters: Steady churn where each exit is followed by an arrival of similar length
In the online trace, prompts are 22K-45K tokens and every slot already holds at least that much, so many reuses may need little or no new mapping
Short per-iteration gaps that let the background thread prepare the next reqId in time
do_not_infer: Do not infer that the paper measured the reuse hit rate; it reports none
Do not infer that deferred reclamation fails in online serving; it may hit often there
Do not infer that the 1.03x-1.15x overhead is incurred in every burst

candidates.headline: No observed TLB thrashing with 64KB pages does not imply or guarantee that small pages are harmless for other kernels or GPUs
candidates.claim: The paper's 'no TLB thrashing' result for small page-groups rests on the regular access pattern of the tested attention kernels. It is not a general property of 64KB pages, and it was measured on A100 only.
candidates.paper_fact: We attribute this to the regular computation pattern of the attention operator as well as the hand-tuned implementations that explicitly try to avoid irregular memory accesses.
candidates.premise: TLB reach is entries times page size, so 64KB pages cover 32x less address space per entry than 2MB pages. Whether that matters depends on how much address space a kernel touches within a short window. TLB and page-table geometry differ across GPU generations.
candidates.inference: By the authors' own attribution, the harmlessness of small pages is conditional on regular, streaming access. A kernel with scattered access, such as sparse or paged-like attention, could exceed TLB reach and lose performance. The A100 result may not carry over to GPUs with different TLB geometry. This consequence is inferred and was not tested in the paper.
candidates.toy_example: Illustrative only, not a measurement: a kernel that touches 1,000 distinct 64KB pages per short window needs 1,000 TLB entries. The same footprint at 2MB needs about 32 entries. If the TLB holds fewer than 1,000 entries, the 64KB case misses repeatedly while the 2MB case does not.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If a deployed kernel has irregular access or the GPU has a smaller or different TLB, the 64KB configuration could show a slowdown that Figure 14 does not capture.
candidates.critical_link: Regular streaming access in the tested kernels is what keeps the number of live translations within TLB reach.
necessary_conditions: The attention kernel streams through the KV cache regularly.
TLB and page-table geometry resembles the A100's.
Kernel runtime in isolation is the relevant metric.
defeaters: Irregular, sparse or paged-like access patterns.
A different GPU generation with different TLB reach.
A different kernel implementation that does not avoid irregular accesses.
do_not_infer: Do not infer that the authors' measurements are wrong.
Do not infer that small pages actually thrash on any specific kernel or GPU.
Do not infer that the Llama-3-70B and GPT-3-175B result fails; the paper reports it as consistent.
candidates.lens: L1+L5: scope of the TLB result across kernels and architectures
